title: Das junggeglühte Männlein
titleEn: The Old Man Made Young Again
part: The Old Man Made Young Again
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 147. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (gieng, geschahs, Deß, dirs).
about: KHM 147 has our Lord and Saint Peter on the road again, as in several of the Grimms' legendary tales, this time lodging with a smith and restoring a broken old beggar to youth by burning him in the forge fire and quenching him in a trough. The smith, sure he has watched closely enough to repeat the trick, tries it on his own mother-in-law — with the gruesome results such imitation tales always deliver. It belongs to the small cluster of Kinderlegenden-like stories where holy power is shown to be exactly not a technique the greedy can copy.

sentences.t: Zur Zeit da unser Herr noch auf Erden gieng, kehrte er eines Abends mit dem heiligen Petrus bei einem Schmied ein und bekam willig Herberge.
sentences.l: At the time when our Lord still walked upon earth, he turned in one evening with Saint Peter at a smith’s and was given lodging willingly.
sentences.i: In the days when our Lord still walked the earth, he stopped one evening at a smith’s house with Saint Peter, and was given lodging willingly.
sentences.n: “Zur Zeit da …” is the old way of saying “at the time when”; modern German would want “als.” “einkehren” is a separable verb (kehrte … ein): to turn in somewhere for the night. “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging. The tale belongs to the legends in which Christ and Saint Peter wander the country on foot and lodge with ordinary people.

sentences.t: Nun geschahs, daß ein armer Bettelmann, von Alter und Gebrechen hart gedrückt, in dieses Haus kam und vom Schmied Almosen forderte.
sentences.l: Now it happened that a poor beggar-man, hard pressed by age and infirmity, came into this house and asked alms of the smith.
sentences.i: Now it came to pass that a poor beggar-man, sorely burdened by age and infirmity, came into the house and asked the smith for alms.
sentences.n: “geschahs” is “geschah es” with the pronoun clipped onto the verb — the 1857 text does this constantly (you will meet “schobs,” “ers,” “dirs” below). “daß” is the old spelling of dass. “das Gebrechen” is bodily infirmity, the frailty of the old; “fordern” here is simply to ask for, without the sharpness of the modern word.

sentences.t: Deß erbarmte sich Petrus und sprach „Herr und Meister, so dirs gefällt, heil ihm doch seine Plage, daß er sich selbst sein Brot möge gewinnen.“
sentences.l: Of that Peter took pity and spoke “Lord and Master, if it please you, do heal him his affliction, so that he may gain his own bread himself.”
sentences.i: Peter was moved to pity at this and said, “Lord and Master, if it please you, heal him of his affliction, that he may earn his own bread.”
sentences.n: “Deß” is the old genitive of das, and “sich erbarmen” governs the genitive — literally “took pity of that.” “so dirs gefällt” is “so es dir gefällt,” an old conditional with so where modern German uses wenn. “möge” is the subjunctive of mögen, the polite old “may”; “sein Brot gewinnen” is to win, that is to earn, one’s bread. The “doch” in “heil ihm doch” is the coaxing particle — “do heal him.”

sentences.t: Sanftmüthig sprach der Herr „Schmied, leih mir deine Esse und lege mir Kohlen an, so will ich den alten kranken Mann zu dieser Zeit verjüngen.“
sentences.l: Mildly spoke the Lord “Smith, lend me your forge-hearth and lay coals on for me, then I will make the old sick man young again at this hour.”
sentences.i: Gently the Lord said, “Smith, lend me your forge and lay on the coals for me, and I will make the old sick man young again here and now.”
sentences.n: “sanftmüthig” is the 1857 spelling of sanftmütig, gentle of temper. “die Esse” is the smith’s hearth, the fire-place of the forge, and the forge vocabulary carries the whole tale. “anlegen” is separable (lege … an): to lay on, to build up a fire. “so will ich” — the so answers the command: “then I will.” “zu dieser Zeit” means on the spot, here and now.

sentences.t: Der Schmied war ganz bereit, und St. Petrus zog die Bälge,
sentences.l: The smith was quite ready, and St. Peter pulled the bellows,
sentences.i: The smith was entirely willing, and Saint Peter worked the bellows,
sentences.n: “die Bälge” is the plural of der Balg: German counts a forge-bellows as several. “St.” is the abbreviation of Sankt, Saint. “bereit sein” is to be ready and willing.

sentences.t: und als das Kohlenfeuer auffunkte, groß und hoch, nahm unser Herr das alte Männlein, schobs in die Esse, mitten ins rothe Feuer, daß es drin glühte wie ein Rosenstock, und Gott lobte mit lauter Stimme.
sentences.l: and when the coal-fire flared up, great and high, our Lord took the old little-man, shoved him into the forge-hearth, into the middle of the red fire, so that he glowed in it like a rose-bush, and [he] praised God with a loud voice.
sentences.i: and when the coal fire flared up great and high, our Lord took the old little man and thrust him into the forge, right into the middle of the red fire, so that he glowed there like a rose-bush and praised God in a loud voice.
sentences.n: “auffunken” is to spark up, flare up (separable auf-); “schobs” = schob es; “rothe” is the 1857 spelling of rote. In the last clause “Gott” is the object and no subject is named at all, so the literal supplies [he] in square brackets. Whose voice it is, is genuinely open: the grammar would allow the Lord, who governs the preceding verbs, while the sense favours the glowing man in the fire, praising God out of the flames. This reading takes the little man; the German does not say. “glühen” — to glow — is the verb behind the title: junggeglüht, made young by being brought to a glow.

sentences.t: Nachdem trat der Herr zum Löschtrog, zog das glühende Männlein hinein, daß das Wasser über ihn zusammenschlug, und nachdem ers fein sittig abgekühlt, gab er ihm seinen Segen:
sentences.l: After that the Lord stepped to the quenching-trough, drew the glowing little-man into it, so that the water beat together over him, and after he had cooled him down nice and gently, he gave him his blessing:
sentences.i: Then the Lord stepped to the quenching trough and drew the glowing little man into it, so that the water closed over him; and when he had cooled him properly and gently, he gave him his blessing:
sentences.n: The first “Nachdem” stands alone as an adverb, “after that,” where modern German would want danach; the second is the ordinary conjunction “after.” The Löschtrog is the water-trough beside every forge in which hot iron is quenched — the old man is being handled exactly like a worked piece of metal. “zusammenschlagen” is separable: the water beat together over him. “ers” = er es.

sentences.t: siehe, zuhand sprang das Männlein heraus, zart, gerade, gesund, und wie von zwanzig Jahren.
sentences.l: behold, at once the little-man sprang out, tender, straight, sound, and as of twenty years.
sentences.i: and behold, straightaway the little man sprang out, fresh, straight and sound, and looking twenty years old.
sentences.n: “siehe” is the old imperative “behold,” the storyteller pointing at what comes next. “zuhand” is an old word for at once, on the spot (modern sofort). “wie von zwanzig Jahren” describes his apparent age: like a man of twenty.

sentences.t: Der Schmied, der eben und genau zugesehen hatte, lud sie alle zum Nachtmahl.
sentences.l: The smith, who had watched exactly and closely, invited them all to the night-meal.
sentences.i: The smith, who had watched the whole thing exactly and closely, invited them all to supper.
sentences.n: “eben” here is not the modern particle “just” but the older adjective sense, exact, even — paired with genau it means he watched with precision, which is what persuades him he can copy the trick. “zusehen” is separable (hatte … zugesehen); “das Nachtmahl” is the evening meal, supper. “laden zu” is to invite to.

sentences.t: Er hatte aber eine alte halbblinde bucklichte Schwieger die machte sich zum Jüngling hin und forschte ernstlich ob ihn das Feuer hart gebrennet habe.
sentences.l: But he had an old half-blind hunchbacked mother-in-law, and she made her way over to the young man and inquired earnestly whether the fire had burnt him hard.
sentences.i: But he had an old, half-blind, hunchbacked mother-in-law, and she made her way over to the young man and asked him in earnest whether the fire had burnt him badly.
sentences.n: “die Schwieger” is the old short form of Schwiegermutter. “bucklicht” is bucklig, hunchbacked, with the old -icht ending. There is no comma before “die machte sich … hin”: the relative pronoun simply picks her up again, and English has to say “and she.” “gebrennet” is the older form of gebrannt; “hart” as an adverb means severely.

sentences.t: Nie sei ihm besser gewesen antwortete jener, er habe da in der Glut gesessen wie in einem kühlen Thau.
sentences.l: Never had it been better for him, answered that one; he had sat there in the glowing coals as in a cool dew.
sentences.i: He had never felt better, the young man answered; he had sat there in the embers as though in a cool dew.
sentences.n: The answer is reported speech, and German marks it with the subjunctive — “sei,” “habe” — where English needs “he said that …”; this is everywhere in the tales. “jener” is “that one,” pointing back to the young man. “Thau” is the 1857 spelling of Tau, dew. Note the dative of the person in “nie sei ihm besser gewesen”: it was never better to him.

sentences.t: Was der Jüngling gesagt hatte, das klang die ganze Nacht in den Ohren der alten Frau,
sentences.l: What the young man had said, that rang the whole night in the ears of the old woman,
sentences.i: What the young man had said rang the whole night through in the old woman’s ears,
sentences.n: German likes to put a clause first and then take it up again with “das”; English drops the resuming word. Of a remark, “klingen” means that it keeps sounding, that it stays in the ear.

sentences.t: und als der Herr frühmorgens die Straße weiter gezogen war und dem Schmied wohl gedankt hatte, meinte dieser er könnte seine alte Schwieger auch jung machen, da er fein ordentlich alles mit angesehen habe, und es in seine Kunst schlage.
sentences.l: and when the Lord had early in the morning moved on further along the road and had thanked the smith well, this one thought he could make his old mother-in-law young too, since he had looked on at everything nice and properly, and it fell within his craft.
sentences.i: and when the Lord had gone on his way down the road early in the morning, with good thanks to the smith, the smith thought that he could make his old mother-in-law young as well, since he had watched the whole business closely enough, and it lay within his own trade.
sentences.n: “dieser” — “this one” — points at the last person named, the smith; German uses it where English repeats the name. “mit ansehen” is separable, to look on at something. “es schlage in seine Kunst” is an old idiom: it falls into his art, it belongs to his trade. The subjunctives (könnte, habe, schlage) mark the whole thing as the smith’s own reasoning, reported rather than vouched for.

sentences.t: Rief sie deshalb an, ob sie auch wie ein Mägdlein von achtzehn Jahren in Sprüngen daher wollte gehen.
sentences.l: [He] therefore called out to her, [asking] whether she too would like to go along in leaps like a little maid of eighteen years.
sentences.i: So he called out to her, asking whether she too would like to go skipping about like a girl of eighteen.
sentences.n: The sentence has no subject at all — the storyteller simply drops “er,” and does it again twice below (“Machte also der Schmied,” “Zog damit die Bälge”); the literal supplies [He] and the verb of asking in square brackets. “anrufen” is separable (rief … an), here to call out to someone. “Mägdlein” is the diminutive of Magd, a young girl; “in Sprüngen gehen” is to go with a spring in the step.

sentences.t: Sie sprach „von ganzem Herzen,“ weil es dem Jüngling auch so sanft angekommen war.
sentences.l: She spoke “from a whole heart,” because it had come upon the young man so gently as well.
sentences.i: She said, “With all my heart,” because it had gone so gently with the young man.
sentences.n: “von ganzem Herzen” is the set phrase, with all one’s heart. “ankommen” with a dative person means to come over someone, to affect them: the treatment had felt mild to the young man, so she expects the same.

sentences.t: Machte also der Schmied große Glut und stieß die Alte hinein, die sich hin und wieder bog und grausames Mordgeschrei anstimmte.
sentences.l: Made then the smith a great blaze and thrust the old woman in, who bent this way and that and struck up dreadful murder-screaming.
sentences.i: So the smith made a great blaze and thrust the old woman in, and she writhed this way and that and set up a dreadful screaming as if she were being murdered.
sentences.n: Another verb-first sentence with the subject left out; the literal keeps the German order. “hin und wieder” here is not “now and then” but literally this way and that. “Mordgeschrei anstimmen” — to strike up a murder-cry — is the ordinary phrase for screaming as though being killed; “anstimmen” is separable and properly means to strike up a song.

sentences.t: „Sitz still, was schreist und hüpfst du, ich will erst weidlich zublasen.“
sentences.l: “Sit still, what are you screaming and hopping for, I will first blow at it thoroughly.”
sentences.i: “Sit still — what are you screaming and jumping about for? I mean to give it a good blast first.”
sentences.n: “was” at the head of a question can mean “why, what for.” “weidlich” is an old adverb: thoroughly, good and properly. “zublasen” is separable, to blow at something with the bellows. The smith’s calm while she burns is the joke of the tale, and it is a cruel one; the 1857 text does not soften it.

sentences.t: Zog damit die Bälge von neuem bis ihr alle Haderlumpen brannten.
sentences.l: Drew therewith the bellows anew until all her rags were burning.
sentences.i: With that he worked the bellows again until every rag on her was alight.
sentences.n: Subject dropped once more. “von neuem” is afresh, again. “Haderlumpen” is a doubled word — Hader and Lumpen both mean rag — so: every last rag she had on. “ihr” is the dative of possession, the German way of saying “her rags.”

sentences.t: Das alte Weib schrie ohne Ruhe, und der Schmied dachte „Kunst geht nicht recht zu,“ nahm sie heraus und warf sie in den Löschtrog.
sentences.l: The old woman screamed without rest, and the smith thought “the art is not going rightly,” took her out and threw her into the quenching-trough.
sentences.i: The old woman screamed without ceasing, and the smith thought, “The craft is not going as it should,” took her out and threw her into the quenching trough.
sentences.n: “das Weib” in 1857 is simply the word for a woman and carries none of the contempt it has today. “zugehen” is separable and impersonal: “es geht nicht recht zu” means things are not going right. “Kunst” here is his craft — the skill he thought he had watched closely enough to copy.

sentences.t: Da schrie sie ganz überlaut, daß es droben im Haus die Schmiedin und ihre Schnur hörten:
sentences.l: Then she screamed quite over-loud, so that up in the house the smith’s-wife and her daughter-in-law heard it:
sentences.i: Then she screamed so very loud that the smith’s wife and her daughter-in-law heard it upstairs in the house:
sentences.n: “die Schmiedin” is the smith’s wife — the -in ending makes the woman of a man’s trade or household. “die Schnur” here is not a cord but the old word for a daughter-in-law (modern Schwiegertochter); the two words are spelled alike, and only the household setting tells you which is meant. “droben” is up there, aloft.

sentences.t: die liefen beide die Stiegen herab, und sahen die Alte heulend und maulend ganz zusammen geschnurrt im Trog liegen, das Angesicht gerunzelt, gefaltet und ungeschaffen.
sentences.l: they both ran down the stairs, and saw the old woman lying in the trough, howling and grumbling, shrivelled quite together, her face wrinkled, folded and misshapen.
sentences.i: The two of them ran down the stairs and saw the old woman lying in the trough, howling and grumbling, shrivelled right up, her face wrinkled, folded and misshapen.
sentences.n: “die Stiegen” are stairs, a flight of steps (die Stiege) — not a form of steigen, which it looks like. “zusammen geschnurrt” is shrunk together, shrivelled; “maulen” is to grumble with the mouth pulled down. “ungeschaffen” means unshapen, ill-made, and it sets up the last word of the tale: what is born that night is likewise “nicht wie Menschen geschaffen.”

sentences.t: Darob sich die zwei, die beide mit Kindern giengen, so entsetzten, daß sie noch dieselbe Nacht zwei Junge gebaren,
sentences.l: At that the two, who both went with child, took such fright that they bore two young ones that very same night,
sentences.i: At this the two women, who were both with child, took such fright that they gave birth that very night to two young ones,
sentences.n: “darob” is the old form of darüber, at that, over that. “mit Kindern gehen” is the old phrase for being pregnant. “sich entsetzen” is to be seized with horror — and folk belief held that a fright in pregnancy marked the child, which is the hinge the joke turns on. “Junge” here is the noun, young ones, offspring, not the adjective “young.”

sentences.t: die waren nicht wie Menschen geschaffen, sondern wie Affen, liefen zum Wald hinein; und von ihnen stammt das Geschlecht der Affen her.
sentences.l: these were not shaped like human beings, but like apes, ran into the wood; and from them the race of the apes descends.
sentences.i: and these were not made in the shape of human beings but of apes; they ran off into the forest, and from them the whole race of apes is descended.
sentences.n: “herstammen” is separable and stands split across the clause (stammt … her): to be descended from. This is an etiological ending — the tale exists to explain where apes came from — and the Grimms print it without a word of comment on the burning that produced them.

glossary.alte: alt — old (infl.; die Alte: the old woman, here the smith’s mother-in-law)
glossary.alter: das Alter — (old) age (von Alter und Gebrechen gedrückt: pressed by age and infirmity)
glossary.angekommen: ankommen — came upon, affected (past part., with the dative of the person: es war ihm sanft angekommen, it had gone gently with him; elsewhere: arrived)
glossary.eben: eben — exactly, precisely (here paired with genau; elsewhere: just, just then)
glossary.fein: fein — nicely, properly (adverbial intensifier: fein sittig, fein ordentlich; elsewhere: fine, delicate)
glossary.gerade: gerade — straight, upright (adj.; here of the man’s body; elsewhere: just, exactly)
glossary.gezogen: ziehen — moved on, travelled (past part. with sein; die Straße weiter ziehen: to go on along the road; elsewhere: pulled, drawn)
glossary.heil: heilen — heal (imperative sg.; heil ihm seine Plage: heal him of his affliction)
glossary.heiligen: heilig — holy, saint (adj., infl.; der heilige Petrus: Saint Peter)
glossary.junge: das Junge — a young one, an animal’s young (pl. Junge; zwei Junge gebaren: bore two young)
glossary.kehrte: einkehren — turned in, put up for the night (3rd sg. past; separable ein-: kehrte … ein)
glossary.kranken: krank — sick, ill (adj., infl.; den alten kranken Mann: the old sick man)
glossary.lauter: laut — loud (adj., infl.; mit lauter Stimme: in a loud voice)
glossary.lege: anlegen — lay on, build up (imperative sg.; the particle waits at the end: lege … an; plain legen: to lay)
glossary.lud: einladen — invited (3rd sg. past; laden zu: to invite to)
glossary.rief: anrufen — called out to (3rd sg. past; the particle waits at the end: rief … an; plain rufen: to call)
glossary.schlage: schlagen — falls, belongs (3rd sg. present subjunctive; in seine Kunst schlagen: to fall within one’s craft)
glossary.sei: sein — be (3rd sg. present subjunctive of reported speech: nie sei ihm besser gewesen, he had never felt better; elsewhere the imperative, be)
glossary.sprüngen: der Sprung — leaps, bounds (dat. pl. Sprüngen; in Sprüngen gehen: to go with a spring in the step)
glossary.st: St. — abbreviation of Sankt, Saint (St. Petrus: Saint Peter)
glossary.stiegen: die Stiege — stairs, flight of steps (pl. Stiegen; die Stiegen herab: down the stairs)
glossary.stieß: stoßen — thrust, shoved (3rd sg. past; stieß die Alte hinein: thrust the old woman in)
glossary.weib: das Weib — woman (in 1857 simply the word for a woman, without the contempt it carries today)
